good: Do not wait for networkidle on a page that carries a polling widget. The support chat widget polls every 20 seconds, so the network is never idle and the wait runs until the 30 second test timeout. Wait for a specific element instead, such as the page heading being visible; the order-history test then finished in about two seconds.
bad: Playwright's networkidle wait is broken, so never use waitForLoadState. Use waitForSelector on the page heading instead, and disable the chat widget in tests.
note: A failure with a clear cause and a fix that worked. A good lesson says why networkidle never settled and what to wait for instead, without turning one polling widget into a ban on networkidle.

good: gh issue list returns only the first 30 results unless --limit is passed, and it gives no warning when it truncates the list, so an audit that counts its output is capped at 30. Pass --limit 200 and treat a result count equal to the limit as possibly truncated. gh pr list has the same default.
bad: All gh list commands are capped, so always paginate with gh api --paginate or use --limit 1000 to get everything.
note: A tool default that silently truncated an audit. A good lesson states the default of 30, the missing warning and the fix, and stays with gh issue list and gh pr list.

good: Converting images to CMYK is not enough for the vendor's preflight: Chromium exports CSS text colours such as #000 as RGB black, so the cover was still rejected with 'RGB content found'. Convert the finished PDF with Ghostscript (-sColorConversionStrategy=CMYK) and run the preflight again.
bad: Every print vendor rejects RGB, so always convert images with ImageMagick and an ICC profile before building the PDF.
note: A rejected file whose cause was not the obvious one. A good lesson names the RGB text colour, the Ghostscript conversion of the finished PDF and the repeated preflight, and does not blame the images.

good: A LiteLLM virtual key's rpm_limit applies to the key as a whole, not to each model, so two models on one key share a single budget. The batch got 429s at about 60 requests a minute although the upstream provider allowed more; giving the classifier its own key with a higher rpm_limit removed them.
bad: LiteLLM rate limits are unreliable, so always set tpm_limit and model_rpm_limit on every key to avoid 429s.
note: A limit that behaved differently from what the batch assumed. A good lesson says the key's limit is shared across models and that a separate key fixed it, without adding other limit types.

good: A service account that gets 404 File not found on files in a shared drive must be a member of the shared drive itself; sharing one folder with it did not help. Adding it as a Viewer member fixed the exports, and the Drive API call also needs supportsAllDrives=true. Its key and scopes did not need to change.
bad: Shared drive exports need domain-wide delegation and an Editor role for the service account, plus the drive scope.
note: An access failure with two separate causes. A good lesson names the shared-drive membership and supportsAllDrives, and does not invent delegation, roles or scopes.

good: A # in an Apprise URL starts a fragment and everything after it is dropped, so a Matrix room alias written as #ops-alerts:example.org addressed no room, and notify.sh printed no error. Write the # as %23. A dry run does not catch this, so confirm with a real test message.
bad: Always percent-encode every special character in every Apprise URL, because Apprise has a bug that silently drops rooms.
note: A silent delivery failure with one specific cause. A good lesson says a # must be written %23, why, and that the failure is silent, without widening it to all special characters.

good: A repository search that finds no references does not prove a function is unused: the nightly job built handler names at runtime from its config, handlers[f'export_{fmt}'], and production still set fmt to legacy_csv. Before deleting a function whose name follows a pattern, search for the prefix and check the config files, not only the full name in code.
bad: Never delete a function based on search results, because text search is unreliable; also check getattr and reflection use.
note: A removal that looked safe and was not. A good lesson says the handler name is built at runtime from config and tells the reader to search for the prefix and the config, without turning it into a rule never to delete.

good: git push --follow-tags pushes annotated tags only, so a lightweight tag made with git tag v2.4.0 stayed local and the tag-triggered release job never started. Create release tags with git tag -a so that --follow-tags pushes them.
bad: Release tags must be GPG-signed, and you should always run git push --tags instead of --follow-tags.
note: A release that silently did not start. A good lesson says --follow-tags pushes annotated tags only and that the lightweight tag stayed local, without adding signing or other push options.

good: On the Paged.js rulebook build, long footnotes were clipped at the bottom margin because a break-inside: avoid rule on the footnote area also applied to the call-out boxes; removing it from .footnote-area fixed page 14. This was verified only on the single-column rulebook; the two-column supplement was not rebuilt.
bad: break-inside: avoid usually causes clipping in Paged.js, so remove it everywhere; the fix works for all layouts including the two-column supplement.
note: A fix checked in one place. A good lesson keeps the scope: the fix was verified on the single-column rulebook only. It must not say the fix holds for all layouts or that the rule usually causes clipping.

good: A Playwright test that failed about one run in five on small CI runners passed 20 runs in a row after retries: 2 was added, but the cause was not found. The suspected slow autocomplete request is untested, and the retries only hide the failures, so the test stays marked @flaky until someone investigates.
bad: Flaky Playwright tests are caused by slow autocomplete requests on small runners; retries fix them, so always add retries to every flaky test.
note: A symptom hidden, not cured. A good lesson says the retries mask the failures and the cause is unknown. It must not present the autocomplete guess as the cause or retries as the cure.

good: In the report-service, upgrading pdfkit-lite from 3.1.4 to 3.2.0 removed the font subset deprecation warning, the tests passed and three sample reports rendered the same in a manual check. The invoice-service still pins 3.1.4 and was not checked, and the rest of the 3.2.0 changelog was not read.
bad: Upgrading pdfkit-lite to 3.2.0 has no breaking changes, so every service can upgrade without checking.
note: One service upgraded and one not checked. A good lesson stays with the report-service result and the unchecked invoice-service. It must not call the upgrade safe or free of breaking changes.

good: On the 40-prompt review set, fast-8b answered in a median of 4.2 seconds against 6.8 seconds for deep-27b, one request at a time on a shared GPU that a labelling job was also using. Answer quality was not compared, and times on an idle server will differ.
bad: fast-8b is faster than deep-27b and gives better quality, so always prefer fast-8b.
note: A timing sample, not a ranking. A good lesson reports the two medians on the 40-prompt set with its conditions. It must not claim better quality or a general preference.

good: A print vendor's preflight accepted a PDF with a 0.125 inch bleed although the vendor's template page asks for 0.25 inch. Nobody asked the vendor about the difference, so it is unconfirmed whether 0.125 inch is enough. The two earlier books used 0.25 inch.
bad: The vendor only requires 0.125 inch bleed, because its template page is out of date, so 0.125 inch is enough for all books.
note: One accepted file, no confirmation. A good lesson reports the accepted 0.125 inch bleed against the 0.25 inch template and says it is unconfirmed. It must not state a new minimum.

good: Lowering PREVIEW_CACHE_TTL on the staging preview server from 3600 to 60 seconds stopped stale previews within a minute and raised CPU use from about 5 percent to about 9 percent. It was tried on staging only and reverted; production still uses 3600, and its CPU cost at ten times the traffic is not known.
bad: A 60 second PREVIEW_CACHE_TTL is safe in production because the CPU impact is negligible, so lower it everywhere.
note: A staging experiment. A good lesson keeps the result on staging: the CPU rise and the unknown production cost. It must not call the change safe for production or its cost negligible.

good:
Export the PDF with the print vendor's own colour profile, not the default one.
A file in the wrong profile comes back from the vendor's preflight with shifted colours.
The profile is set in the export dialog, under the Output tab.
With the default profile the blues of the Hollin Reach cover shifted toward purple.
bad:
Export the PDF with the print vendor's own colour profile, not the default one.
A file in the wrong profile comes back from the vendor's preflight with shifted colours.
The profile is set in the export dialog, under the Output tab.
With the default profile the blues of the Hollin Reach cover shifted toward purple.
The profile is set under the Output tab. Every vendor needs its own profile, and the default is sRGB, which always shifts blues toward purple.
note: The memory restates the lesson's rule and adds where the profile is set and the symptom. A good update keeps both lesson lines and adds those two facts, without claiming that every vendor needs a profile or naming the default one.

good:
Create the data a test needs inside the test, and remove it afterwards.
A test that reads rows another test left behind fails when the order changes.
The runner has sorted the test files by name since version 4.2, which is when the order changed.
bad:
Create the data a test needs inside the test, and remove it afterwards.
A test that reads rows another test left behind fails when the order changes.
The runner has sorted the test files by name since version 4.2, which is when the order changed.
The runner has sorted the test files by name since version 4.2. Run the tests in parallel with a random order, and reset the database between tests.
note: The memory restates the lesson's rule and adds why the order changed: the runner sorts files by name since 4.2. A good update adds that one fact and no fix beyond creating the data in the test.

good:
Link the commit or change that fixes a ticket before closing it.
A ticket closed without a link cannot be checked later.
Finding the fix for TRK-212 by searching the history took an hour.
The tracker's close form requires a link only for tickets labelled regression.
bad:
Link the commit or change that fixes a ticket before closing it.
A ticket closed without a link cannot be checked later.
Finding the fix for TRK-212 by searching the history took an hour.
The tracker's close form requires a link only for tickets labelled regression.
Finding the fix by searching the history took an hour. The close form requires a link for every ticket, and the tracker reopens a ticket automatically when the link is missing.
note: The memory restates the lesson's rule and adds what the missing link cost (an hour) and where the tracker asks for a link (only for regression tickets). A good update adds those facts without making the link mandatory for every ticket.

good:
Name the files a delegated task may touch in the task itself.
A model told only the goal edits files outside the task.
The small model also rewrote two files in the billing module when the task said only to tidy the notifications code.
The large model stayed in scope on the same task without a list.
bad:
Name the files a delegated task may touch in the task itself.
A model told only the goal edits files outside the task.
The small model also rewrote two files in the billing module when the task said only to tidy the notifications code.
The large model stayed in scope on the same task without a list.
The small model rewrote two files in the billing module. All small models stray like this, so every model needs a read-only sandbox and a review of the diff.
note: The memory restates the lesson's rule and adds the damage (two billing files) and a limit (the large model stayed in scope without a list). A good update adds those facts and does not say small models always stray.

good:
Share a Drive file with a group, not with each person.
A person who leaves the team keeps access to the files shared with them directly.
Adding the group did not close the access; removing the direct entry did.
A change to the group reaches the files within about ten minutes.
bad:
Share a Drive file with a group, not with each person.
A person who leaves the team keeps access to the files shared with them directly.
Adding the group did not close the access; removing the direct entry did.
A change to the group reaches the files within about ten minutes.
Remove the direct entry. A change to the group reaches every file instantly, so move all files into shared drives and revoke the OAuth tokens.
note: The memory restates the lesson's rule and adds the step that closed the access (removing the direct entry, not just adding the group) and the delay of a group change (about ten minutes). A good update adds those facts and does not say the change is instant.

good:
Send one alert per incident, not one per failing check.
Repeated alerts for the same incident train people to mute the channel.
During the queue outage the pager sent 41 alerts in 20 minutes.
The alert tool groups by the incident label, and a check with no label is still sent alone.
bad:
Send one alert per incident, not one per failing check.
Repeated alerts for the same incident train people to mute the channel.
During the queue outage the pager sent 41 alerts in 20 minutes.
The alert tool groups by the incident label, and a check with no label is still sent alone.
The pager sent 41 alerts in 20 minutes. The alert tool groups by the incident label and groups across services, so rate limit the pager and snooze the rest.
note: The memory restates the lesson's rule and adds the count (41 alerts in 20 minutes) and how grouping works (the incident label; an unlabelled check is sent alone). A good update adds those facts without proposing a rate limit or escalation.

good:
Check the exit code of every command the script runs, and stop on a non-zero one.
A script that ignores a failed step reports success on a broken result.
The nightly export printed done after its upload failed with exit code 28, a timeout, so the bucket held yesterday's file.
bad:
Check the exit code of every command the script runs, and stop on a non-zero one.
A script that ignores a failed step reports success on a broken result.
The nightly export printed done after its upload failed with exit code 28, a timeout, so the bucket held yesterday's file.
The upload failed with exit code 28, so the bucket held yesterday's file. Retry the upload on every timeout, and set pipefail and email the team on every failure.
note: The memory restates the lesson's rule and adds the exit code (28, a timeout) and the consequence (the bucket held yesterday's file). A good update adds those facts and no retry or alert.

good:
Set headings to keep with the next paragraph.
A heading left at the foot of a page looks like a mistake in print.
Use break-after: avoid on headings.
The property has no effect inside a flex container in Paged.js 0.4.
bad:
Set headings to keep with the next paragraph.
A heading left at the foot of a page looks like a mistake in print.
Use break-after: avoid on headings.
The property has no effect inside a flex container in Paged.js 0.4.
Use break-after: avoid on headings. It never works in flex containers in any browser, so set orphans and widows and break-inside: avoid, or upgrade Paged.js.
note: The memory restates the lesson's rule and adds the property to use and its limit (no effect inside a flex container in Paged.js 0.4). A good update adds those facts and does not generalise the limit.
